newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Official says Russia army reform will be tough.
newsitem.headline: Official says Russia army reform will be tough.

text.p: A Russian senior official said on Saturday that military reform, forced on Moscow through the failure of a struggling national budget to keep up its huge Soviet-era armed forces, will be painful and cannot be rushed.
The secretary of the newly-established Defence Council, Yuri Baturin, told a news conference that the body, which met for the first time on Friday, would spearhead the reform.
"So far the process of change has not been effective enough," Baturin said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, chairing Friday's meeting in the absence of hospital-bound President Boris Yeltsin, said painful steps had to go ahead quickly.
Baturin quoted Chernomyrdin as saying that "concrete, real and unpopular measures" must be taken promptly.
He declined to give details.
A chronic cash shortage, poor living conditions and a lack of clearity about future prospects have caused discontent among much of the military.
Russian security chief Alexander Lebed said last week that the army could be hit by revolts as a result of unpaid wages.
Baturin said he did not believe in the possibility of mutiny unless it were deliberately provoked.
"The military generally stick to discipline," he said. "It would be so unnatural for them to launch a revolt if it is not instigated by someone."

Baturin said that the Kremlin was being forced into military reform without having a proper defence doctrine by the poor shape of the armed forces. But he made clear that he would not favour changes for the sake of changes.
He seemed sceptical about Yeltsin's plan to turn the army into a purely professional force and end conscription by 2000. The president made the pledge in his reelection campaign this spring.

"I rather share the opinion of the defence minister (Igor Rodionov) that this can be done by 2005," he said. "In general I'd like someone to tell me what the Russian economy will look like in two years before making such far-reaching predictions."
Baturin said he was much more worried by prospects of the best officers leaving the army in despair of improvement.
He said that the military reform was aimed at creating armed forces which would be both effective and affordable for the state.
"The main task is to maintaing the capability of the armed forces to fight," Baturin said. "But the state must be able to afford any such solution financially."
Yeltsin on Thursday told the government to resolve cash problems in the army. Many soldiers have been unpaid for months.
"Russia must have a modern and professional army," Yeltsin said in a radio address from the Central Clinical Hospital, where he is getting ready for heart surgery.
The Defence Council meeting examined ways of reorganising the armed forces. Government officials said there were too many generals and too much bureaucracy.
Some changes have already been made.
The Defence Ministry said on Friday that Yeltsin had sacked several senior generals and Russian media said the move showed Rodionov, appointed in July, was ready for action.

Rodionov has announced plans to reduce the army to 1.2 million from about 1.5 million men. Baturin said the least effective units would be disbanded but he was worried that the ranks could be thinned badly as a result of the cash squeeze.
